#1503. O'Neill admits new signings are struggling with demands of being a Celtic player after dispiriting loss at Falkirk

Published: 11:08 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 11:21 EDT, 1 November 2026

Celtic boss Martin O’Neill admitted his summer recruits need to prove that they have the character and quality to handle the pressure of playing for the club.

The league leaders went down 2-0 at Falkirk on Sunday afternoon – their sixth defeat in their last 10 in all competitions – as they missed the chance to extend their advantage at the top of the Premiership table to seven points.

First-half strikes from Ethan Ross and Scott Tanser had the Bairns ahead at the break, and despite peppering Scott Bain’s goal in the second period, the visitors were unable to find a response.

When it was put to O’Neill that some new members of his squad are still struggling to meet the club’s high expectations, he said: ‘Absolutely. You have to cope with the pressure to be a player.

‘Tommy Burns said it might be easier to play against Celtic than for Celtic but hopefully we have enough in the dressing room and players who have been big winners.

‘When you ask managers sometimes you think the best team is the one that has won convincingly, but there are a number of players who have arrived.

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill was unhappy with his team's defending at Falkirk

‘You can think someone is doing well in training but the only place to find where players fit is out there.

‘We’re not used to losing a lot of games. We were in a much worse position this time last year so we have to buckle down and win a game and win a game in Europe. Thursday [against Besiktas in the Europa League] is a big game and then the following Sunday is massive before we go into the international break.

‘We need to sort out a few things. I was asked about confidence. If you take Kasper [Hogh], he wanted to get a goal after some time.

‘Something might fall for him but it’s not just that something might fall for you. You have to work at it which is something us as a team and the players in particular need to do.’

O’Neill bemoaned the defensive lapses that allowed Falkirk to open up a two-goal cushion, but saw enough in his team’s performance in the attacking third to give him confidence that things will soon start clicking.

‘I’m naturally disappointed to have lost the game,’ he said. ‘We had a lot of chances. Their goalie was magnificent but naturally we’ve lost so I’m very disappointed.

Callum McGregor looks frustrated as Celtic are made to suffer in Falkirk

‘The goals were very poor from our viewpoint. We didn’t clear it for the first one then we let someone run through and pick his spot for the second. We had some really great chances we just weren’t able to convert.

‘At half-time I thought we were still in the game. I thought we’d played decent stuff. If you concede a magnificent goal you take it in your stride.

‘When you concede a bad goal, which from any viewpoint was a poor goal, then it’s tough to come back then the goalie makes some saves and it’s frustrating.

‘Despite mistakes at the back we had enough chances to get back.

‘We have conceded some poor goals and haven’t kept a clean sheet for some time which is the essence of a championship team, but we’re still top and we need to address it and that’s the way out of it.

‘We scored seven against Hearts which isn’t that long ago. I just thought the goalie had a magnificent game and we should have scored a number in each half.

‘When you don’t it becomes frustrating. We have to address that we were conceding. Hopefully we can still do that. It’s still a long season.’

#1498. The top 10 goalscorers in Europe in the 2020s: Mbappe vs Haaland for top spot, Salah 5th…

Which players have scored the most goals in Europe’s top five leagues in the 2020s?

The 2010s were dominated by Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, but neither are playing in Europe anymore and didn’t get enough goals before they left to stay in the top 10 scorers of the decade.

There are plenty of familiar names in the current top 10 though, with the three leading scorers separated by just three goals.

Here are the 10 players with the most goals across the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 since the turn of the decade.

Schick knocked ex-Aston Villa striker Ollie Watkins out of the top 10 in October.

He began the 2020s on loan at RB Leipzig from Roma, but went on to find his home at Leverkusen, where’s he’s now closing in on 100 league goals.

Alexander Isak is catching up with him, but Schick is just ahead for now.

After emerging in European football with a prolific spell at Gent, David joined Lille in the summer of 2020.

Over the next five seasons in Ligue 1, 87 goals by the Canada international followed.

He found things a bit tougher in Serie A after joining Juventus in 2025, only scoring six times from 36 league outings so far.

Juventus have sent him on loan to Atletico Madrid for this season and he scored on his La Liga debut.

Arguably the least household name here, Budimir plays for Osasuna and has only ever made it to the play-off rounds of a European competition (the 2023-24 Conference League).

But the 41-cap, seven-goal Croatia international has showcased his reliability in La Liga over the past few seasons, hitting double figures in 2020-21, 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26.

Only Kylian Mbappe and Robert Lewandowski – spoiler alert, but those are two names you’ll be seeing again later – outscored Budimir in La Liga in the 2024-25 season. Then in 2025-26, only Mbappe and the relegated Mallorca frontman Vedat Muriqi scored more.

Now 35, Budimir might not have too much time left at the top level, but is under contract with Osasuna for the rest of the season.

Now 30 years old, Guirassy has played exclusively in France and Germany during his career so far.

He began the 2020s in Ligue 1 with Amiens, but suffered relegation at the end of the 2019-20 season before moving back into the top flight with Rennes.

Whilst with Rennes, he added another 19 Ligue 1 goals to his five from the second half of 2019-20.

A move to Germany with Stuttgart followed in 2022, leading to 39 Bundesliga goals in two years. He came one shy of reaching the same amount from his first two seasons with Borussia Dortmund.

Martinez has been with Inter Milan since the summer of 2018, which means his debut season in Serie A was the only one that didn’t span into any of the 2020s.

It was also the only one in which he has failed to hit double figures of goals. The Argentine striker even enjoyed three consecutive seasons with 20+ goals between 2021-22 and 2023-24, ranking as Serie A’s top scorer for the latter.

Martinez has often played as part of a strike partnership at Inter, but his longevity enables him to outrank colleagues past and present like Romelu Lukaku, Edin Dzeko and Marcus Thuram for goals since the start of the decade.

Salah left Liverpool in the summer for Trabzonspor, marking the end (for now) of his goal-getting in Europe’s top leagues.

He was extraordinary in front of goal after joining Liverpool in 2017, being able to boast 128 Premier League goals in the 2020s alone.

During that time, he claimed two Golden Boots, including from the 2024-25 season when Liverpool won the league.

He should be staying in this top 10 long after his departure from Liverpool thanks to the collection of goals he has already built up.

Lewandowski denied Erling Haaland the chance to win a Golden Boot in the Bundesliga while maintaining outlandish levels of form for Bayern Munich.

Lewandowski then began firing them in for Barcelona, where he moved in 2022. More than 80 La Liga goals followed.

Now at the age of 38, Lewandowski only scored 14 times in the league last season, but has proven wrong anyone who may have doubted his ability to keep scoring regularly at this stage of his career.

The winner of the European Golden Shoe in each of his last two seasons with Bayern, Lewandowski was La Liga’s top scorer in his first with Barcelona.

He is now playing outside of Europe for Chicago Fire in MLS.

Kane has 99 Bundesliga goals to his name from 97 games since joining Bayern Munich in 2023 and was top of this ranking by the end of last season.

Before his spell with Bayern, he enjoyed some prolific seasons towards the end of his time in the Premier League with Tottenham Hotspur, including 30 in his last season.

The 33-year-old is in the final season of his contract with Bayern but is showing no signs of slowing down, even breaking the 60-goal barrier in all competitions last season.

Haaland is still behind Salah in the Premier League scoring chart for the 2020s, but his exploits in the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund from the start of the decade place him 50-odd goals above the Liverpool legend here.

Haaland entered Europe’s top five leagues by joining Dortmund in January 2020 and proceeded to score 62 Bundesliga goals from 67 games prior to his move to Manchester City.

The big Norwegian striker was in no mood to slow his scoring rate in England, setting a new Premier League record for most goals in a 38-game season at the first time of asking with 36 (from just 35 appearances).

Haaland shattered through the landmark of 100 Premier League goals during the 2025-26 season and at the age of 26, should still have plenty more goals up his sleeve in the years to come.

Mbappe will most likely be going toe to toe with Haaland over the next few years to finish in top spot.

By the time he left PSG in 2024, Mbappe had become the French club’s all-time record scorer. A move to Real Madrid followed and he went on to score a Pichichi-worthy 31 goals in his first La Liga season.

Mbappe finished with 25 to his name in his second – again being La Liga’s top scorer – which meant he was recently able to pass a half-century of La Liga goals. He will be hungry for more (and silverware) over the coming seasons.

#1497. Can you name Leeds United’s XI from their 4-3 win over Liverpool in 2000?

You probably don’t need to look at the above picture to remember who scored all four goals in Leeds United‘s unforgettable 4-3 victory over Liverpool in November 2000 – but do you know the rest of David O’Leary’s side that day?

It was an individual display destined to be talked about for decades to come by Leeds’ No.9 that afternoon, but the supporting cast wasn’t bad either: this was a side that famously made it all the way to the Champions League semi-finals that season.

“We felt invincible as a club at that time,” said one former midfielder who started for Leeds on that November afternoon. “We attacked every game, we were impossible to play against. We were aggressive and entertaining. We believed we could beat anyone.”

Gerard Houllier’s Liverpool would go on to have the last laugh, winning three trophies in 2000-01 and pipping Leeds to third by just a point. “What happened next was awful,” another Leeds man remembered. “We missed out [on the Champions League] by one point, and from there the finances became a mess.”

But that day undoubtedly belonged to the Yorkshire side. So we’re asking you to name O’Leary’s starting XI. The time to beat from the Leeds fan in the Planet Football office is 00:56.

And if this gives you the taste for another quiz, why not try naming every player that featured in Leeds’ run to the Champions League semi-final in 2000-01?

#1495. HEARTS 1-2 HIBS - PLAYER RATINGS: Which midfielder ran the show at Hampden? Who missed chances to force extra time?

Published: 12:59 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 13:09 EDT, 1 November 2026

Hibs ripped up the form book to  claim a thrilling victory over city rivals Hearts in  the Premier Sports Cup semi-final at Hampden.

Despite falling behind to an early header by Claudio Braga, the Premiership's bottom-placed side came roaring back with goals from Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

Hearts piled on the second-half pressure, but Marink Reedijk's side held firm to secure a place in the final against Rangers next month.

After a dramatic derby that will be remembered for years to come, Paul Forsyth assesses the individual performances.

Blameless for the two goals, he did his best to repel Hibs with a string of saves. Denied Passlack, Boyle and, in the closing stages, Klidge.

Had his hands full when Boyle threatened to run riot, but stuck to his task. Supported the attack well when Hearts grew desperate.

Caught flat-footed and square when Boyle stole in behind him to net Hibs’ equaliser. Otherwise solid enough when the pressure was on.

Man of the match Joe Newell celebrates with Jamie McGrath after their  team go 2-1 ahead

Bust a gut to cover and thwart Hibs’ explosive breaks. Produced a number of excellent blocks, most notably one that denied Elding.

Stood up well when Hearts needed him. His outstanding sliding block to thwart Passlack late in the game was as good as a goal.

Left the field after just 14 minutes with a horrible head knock, picked up when he nodded Calvin Miller’s cross narrowly wide.

Outnumbered in the first half, he looked lost in midfield. Far more influential when Hearts later got a grip of that department.

Stretched his opponents as Hearts grew into the game, but never really came up with a telling pass or effort on goal.

Caused all sorts of problems with his early crosses, only to become the latest addition to Hearts’ ridiculous injury list. Hobbled off before the interval.

Quiet in the first half, save for a perfect cross that Braga should have converted. Direct, dangerous and back to his best after the interval.

Claudio Braga misses a late chance to force extra time in the Premier Sports Cup semi-final

Opened the scoring from close range, but could and should have done more. Missed two free headers and had a powerful shot saved.

SUBSTITUTES: Wilson (Dhanda 83) (Magnusson 14), Guendouz (Miller 37), Benjaminsen (Kerjota 81)

Unused: Fulton, Williams, Kabore, Findlay, Pollock.

Nowhere to be seen when Braga nodded Hearts ahead from inside the six-yard box, but two saves, denying Braga and Guendouz, were massive.

Aggressive, positive and willing to give Hibs width in attack. Should have scored with an early chance after he was set up by Newell.

Fell asleep for Braga’s early opener, but settled into the game and was a pillar of Hibs’ defence when the pressure mounted.

Switched off to allow Braga a free header that slipped wide. His powerful header at the other end was directed straight at the goalkeeper.

Took full advantage of the early freedom he was given wide on the left. Responded well to later pressure, especially with a brilliant tackle on Kerjota.

Properly exploited Hearts’ depleted midfield with a strong, authoritative first-half display. Less influential after Hearts tweaked their set-up.

His positive, probing work was crucial to Hibs’ first-half dominance. Clipped the top of the crossbar with one shot. Set up his team’s second goal with another.

Strong and tactically aware. By stepping inside, he increased the midfield numbers, allowing McGrath to push forward and Passlack to overlap.

Playing off the front, he supported Elding at every opportunity. Reacted well to snap up the rebound for Hibs’ second.

Martin Boyle equalises for Hibs with a low shot that goes in off the goalkeeper and post

Inspirational talisman in attack. Transformed the game with a timely equaliser, which he stroked in off the goalkeeper and post. Almost scored a second.

Occupied Hearts’ backline without offering a sustained goal threat. His lovely hook over a square defence set up Boyle for the equaliser.

SUBSTITUTES: Klidge (Elding 74), Wright (Newell 74), Cadden (Boyle 85), Hanley (McGrath 85).

Unused: Smith, Iredale, Suto, Matondo, Abdulai.

Failed to cope with the early loss of Tomas Magnusson, which turned the game.

Gave his side numerical superiority in midfield, as well as the resources later  to protect their lead.

#1494. Ranking our 10 favourite Champions League comebacks ever after Man Utd 3-2 Roma

Manchester United’s thrilling 3-2 win over Roma was the kind of comeback to be spoken about for years – but it doesn’t quite make our top 10 in Champions League history.

United were two goals down at half-time, before a stirring second-half performance that probably saved Michael Carrick’s job for another week or two.

We’ve ranked our 10 favourite Champions League comebacks of all time, starting in Catalonia with pre-Abramovich Chelsea beginning to pinch themselves…

Finishing 3rd in the Premier League in 1999 was a big deal for Chelsea, who’d only won a single league title in the 1950s.

Getting to the Champions League quarter-finals and beating Barcelona 3-1 in the first leg was dreamland territory.

But Barca were stacked at the turn of the millennium, with Ballon d’Or winner Rivaldo and pre-pig head Luis Figo running the show.

Both Rivaldo and Figo scored at Camp Nou, before Tore Andre Flo pulled one back to edge Chelsea towards the semis.

They almost made it too. There were just eight minutes remaining when Dani took the game to extra-time, before Rivaldo and Patrick Kluivert made it 5-1.

Chelsea would have their revenge 12 years later, but this was a humbling night.

Early 2004 was peak Galactico Madrid, just before it all fell apart.

Figo, Ronaldo, Zidane, Beckham and Raul all featured in their 4-2 quarter-final win over Monaco, a surely unassailable lead to take into the second leg.

But assembling all those Galacticos meant several talented players became collateral damage, including Fernando Morientes. Madrid had loaned him to Monaco for the 2003-04 season, unaware of the potential narrative ramifications.

His goal, alongside two from the wonderful Ludovic Giuly, ensured the Ligue 1 side won the second leg 3-1 and progressed on away goals.

Real Madrid wouldn’t make another Champions League quarter-final for seven years.

Some might call Chelsea’s run to Champions League glory in 2012 the spawniest of all time, but it was really the culmination of years of grit and sheer bloody-mindedness.

The kind of bloody-mindedness that chewed up and spat out Andre Villas-Boas, the young manager unequipped to lead a dressing room containing John Terry, Frank Lampard and Didier Drogba.

One of Villas-Boas’ last matches was a 3-1 defeat at Napoli, seemingly kiboshing their Champions League hopes.

But Roberto Di Matteo took interim charge of the return leg and the players took it upon themselves to save their season.

Drogba, Terry and Lampard all scored to take the tie to extra time at Stamford Bridge, before Branislav Ivanovic’s dramatic winner sent Chelsea through.

If Ousmane Dembele had scored an easy chance at the end of the first leg, Barcelona would’ve taken a four-goal lead to Anfield.

Instead, it was only 3-0 and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool smelt blood. Divock Origi began the comeback inside seven minutes, before Andy Robertson ruffled Messi’s head.

Georginio Wijnaldum scored a quickfire double to turn the game into one of *those* nights, before a corner was taken quickly, or something.

Surely the greatest night in Tottenham Hotspur’s recent history – even winning the Europa League couldn’t have provided a rush quite like this.

Especially as the situation looked so unpromising. Ajax had cut a swathe through the Champions League that year, won the first leg in London 1-0 and scored two more in Amsterdam to stretch clear.

Enter Lucas Moura. One of those classic Spurs players who flattered to deceive, Moura scored an incredible hat-trick with the final goal coming in the sixth minute of injury time.

Club legend Glenn Hoddle had suffered a heart attack less than a year before this match. In the BT Sport studio, he remarked how glad he was to have seen it and everyone starting welling up.

Barcelona looked to have this quarter-final tie sewn up in the first leg after Gerard Pique and Luis Suarez added to own goals from Daniele de Rossi and Kostas Manolas.

But Edin Dzeko’s consolation in Spain proved to be crucial as Roma won the second leg by an improbable scoreline of 3-0.

Dzeko put Roma ahead after just six minutes, before a De Rossi penalty and a Manolas header atoned for their Nou Camp mistakes.

The one downside is that Peter Drury’s commentary of Manolas’ clincher went viral and now he’s assaulting our ears on a weekly basis.

The most glorious and life-affirming comeback of all? Probably.

One-nil down as the clock ticked into injury-time, Manchester United had played well within themselves on the biggest stage of all.

Mario Basler’s early goal had given Bayern a lead they’d sat on comfortably all match. Then a corner was taken, Peter Schmeichel’s presence in the box caused mayhem and Teddy Sheringham poked home.

Extra-time beckoned, but United were in the zone. Minutes later, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer had won it, Bayern players collapsed to the floor in despair and football had probably peaked.

Milan started like a greyhound out of the traps, an early Paolo Maldini strike giving the Italians the lead. Brazilian attacking midfielder Kaka then turned on the style and by half-time, he had set up two goals for Hernan Crespo to give Milan a seemingly comfortable 3-0 margin.

But Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez made a big change at the break, bringing on Dietmar Hamann and altering Liverpool’s formation. The decision paid off.

The Reds scored three goals in six wild second-half minutes (Gerrard, Smicer, Alonso), before winning 3-2 in a dramatic penalty shootout that became famous for Jerzy Dudek’s theatrics.

Istanbul has never seen a bigger miracle before or since.

The greatest comeback of all is so iconic that it has its very own title in France and Spain – La Remontada.

PSG took a 4-0 lead to the second leg of this last 16 clash in Spain, only for Luis Suarez to open the scoring for Barcelona in three minutes. Game on.

Barcelona were two goals up at half-time after Layvin Kurzawa’s own goal and Lionel Messi scored a penalty to make it three.

Then, a plot twist. Edinson Cavani hit back to silence Camp Nou, although PSG seemed to go into their shells thereafter.

Needing three goals with two minutes of normal time left, Neymar stepped up to the plate in a way he’d never do again.

The Brazilian scored a free-kick and penalty, before a gorgeous chipped pass found Sergi Roberto to incredibly make it 6-1.

Barcelona became the only team to overturn a foul-goal Champions League deficit. Phowar.

#1493. Roma to pursue Kvernadze in January

Roma continues to monitor Giorgi Kvernadze, the Georgian striker currently playing for Frosinone.

The player was reportedly in the Roman club’s sights last summer and will continue to be monitored ahead of the upcoming transfer window.

This interest could become more concrete in the coming months, especially given the player’s financial terms.

The 2003-born striker is tied to Frosinone by a deal valid until June 30, 2028, but his contract reportedly contains a specific release clause.

The fee required to release the striker is reportedly €4 million, with the option to exercise the option next summer.

This valuation could make the Georgian an attractive prospect for Roma, who are keen to monitor various prospects to strengthen their attacking line.

However, the potential deal would present another financial aspect to consider.

As reported by Gazzetta Regionale, in addition to the €4 million stipulated in the release clause, a significant percentage would need to be considered for the player’s agent.

This detail could impact the overall cost of the deal and the Roma management’s assessment.

Kvernadze’s agent is the same one representing Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, another Georgian talent who has established himself in our Serie A. At the moment, Roma’s interest remains to be monitored, and no official negotiations have been initiated to bring Kvernadze to the capital.

#1492. Ranking the 10 right-backs in world football right now: Who are the closest to matching Achraf Hakimi?

The title of world’s best right-back isn’t up for much debate, but the race for the remaining places is fiercely contested.

Europe’s elite are packed with top-class options, with stars from Arsenal, Barcelona, Tottenham, Chelsea and Real Madrid among the standouts. Some thrive as attacking outlets, others excel defensively, while the very best manage to do both.

Here’s our ranking of the 10 best right-backs in world football right now.

There’s something of a Reece James mk.II about Livramento.

Another outstanding Chelsea academy graduate blessed with everything he needs to reach the top, but one whose progress has unfortunately been stunted by injuries.

He’s barely featured this season, with the usual injury issues making it difficult to judge where he’s currently at. But with Newcastle struggling under Matthias Jaissle, the manager could desperately do with a player of Livramento’s quality fit and available.

A safe bet to be England’s starting right-back at the next Euros, provided he can stay on the pitch.

The Italy youth international is already a regular in the transfer gossip columns, but another season of development at Brentford should do him the world of good before the inevitable leap to a Champions League club.

Kayode’s Rory Delap-esque long throws are a fun bonus, but don’t let them overshadow how he already looks like one of the most promising young right-backs in Europe.

Having never managed more than three assists in a league campaign before, Ryerson suddenly turned into one of Europe’s most productive full-backs in the latter half of last season.

The Norwegian ended the 2025-26 Bundesliga season with an outrageous tally of 15 assists, which included four in one game against Mainz.

We’ve seen a reversion to the mean this season, with zero assists to his name, but he’s been solid enough as Dortmund have started in fine fettle, going toe-to-toe with Bayern Munich.

Three La Liga titles. A permanent fixture for France. Another World Cup run deep into the knockout stages. The CV is unquestionable.

But actually watch him play, rather than read his Wikipedia career summary, and you’ll come away with a different impression. Kounde hasn’t looked as assured over the past couple of years as he did at his peak.

He’s still a decent enough right-back, but there are too many switch-offs and untidy moments. Barcelona’s high line is unforgiving, but we still expect more from a player of his ability.

We’re not writing him off, but it’s been a long while since we’ve looked at Kounde and thought of him as one of the outstanding players in his position.

La Masia does it again. Espart has enjoyed an outstanding breakthrough campaign, establishing himself as Hansi Flick’s best right-back and putting Kounde’s place under genuine pressure.

He’s a wonderfully versatile teenager, capable of filling several roles and looking comfortable wherever he’s deployed. His future might ultimately lie further forward in midfield, but for now he’s making the right-back position his own.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is nowhere to be seen in our top 10 right-backs. Some drop-off for a player who boldly stated his ambitions of winning a Ballon d’Or.

We’ve also kicked Denzel Dumfries out of this list for Valverde, who would’ve featured pretty prominently in a midfielders ranking in his prime a couple of years back.

The Los Blancos captain might be playing there reluctantly, which caused a bit of a stir last season, but we find ourselves agreeing with Jose Mourinho.

“It hurts me. Our squad planning was to have two players in each position, and now I’m playing a third guy in their place (Valverde), and that really makes me sad,” the Real Madrid manager said recently.

“In this very specific situation, I think it’s better for the team to play Fede there. I consider Fede a more offensive RB than the other two right now.

“We explained this situation to Trent and Dumfries, and they both accepted it as they understood it’s what best for the team right now.”

READ: Ranking the 10 best midfielders in world football: Rodri, Rice, Vitinha…

Having Porro as high as fourth in this list would’ve felt like a sick joke a few months back.

This is a fella who featured prominently for a Tottenham side that finished 17th in successive Premier League campaigns, with a disastrous defensive record in both.

But this is the danger of judging an individual in a collective context. Stick him in a functional set-up – i.e. Luis de la Fuente’s Spain – and Porro’s quality immediately becomes clear.

He looked every inch the complete right-back at the World Cup: positionally intelligent, defensively assured and a constant threat going forward.

Porro has spent most of this season sidelined, but he’s returning just as Roberto De Zerbi’s side are turning a corner. Watch this space.

There’s an argument that James is too versatile for his own good.

The Chelsea captain can excel in midfield, but that only underlines what an exceptional footballer he is. His best position remains right-back, where few can match his blend of all-round qualities.

Fitness has prevented James from climbing higher. He managed more minutes last season but still missed a significant spell, including much of the World Cup.

Add in Chelsea’s tactical instability and scattergun squad building, and it’s easy to forget just how good he is. If availability wasn’t an issue, and he was playing in a proper team, he’d be challenging for the top two.

Perhaps we’ll see him at his very best under Xabi Alonso this season. But those injury setbacks remain a curse.

Timber’s paltry return in terms of goals and assists is why he isn’t close to the top spot here. He’s never going to be spoken about in the same breath as a Dani Alves or a Cafu.

But with elite attack-minded right-backs in short supply, Timber’s defensive excellence is enough to earn him second place.

Arguably the best one-on-one defender in world football, he was instrumental in Arsenal’s Premier League triumph and coming within a penalty shootout of Champions League glory.

“ACHRAF HAKIMI. BEST RB IN THE WORLD. GOOD NIGHT GUYS. 👋🏽” posted Kylian Mbappe during the 2022 AFCON.

We’ve got a whole series of these rankings. Strikers. Wingers. Centre-backs. In no other position was the No.1 spot so cut and dried.

Hakimi is head and shoulders above the rest. A back-to-back Champions League winner and a key part of Morocco becoming a genuine force in international football.

#1490. Ranking the 10 left-backs in world football right now: Mendes, Cucurella, Calafiori…

Left-backs at Arsenal, PSG, Real Madrid, Inter, Manchester City and Bayern Munich can all be considered to be among the standouts in their position across world football right now.

Whether it’s locking down elite wingers, inverting into midfield or providing width in attack, these are the players doing it better than anyone else.

Here’s our ranking of the 10 best left-backs in world football at this moment in time.

Probably not even the best left/centre-back hybrid at his club, which is more of a statement of the scary defensive depth that Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal are blessed with.

The rugged Ecuadorian is unlikely to ever challenge the assists charts, but he’s remarkably sturdy and reliable.

Few full-backs have ever been as exhilarating as Alphonso Davies in full flight.

We will never forget that electric performance against Barcelona, and desperately hope that isn’t as good as it gets. It’d be a minor footballing tragedy if Davies peaked as a teenager.

Unfortunately, we’re starting to fear that might be the reality. Injuries have certainly disrupted Davies’ progress, and he hasn’t quite looked the same electric presence we’ve come to expect.

There have, however, been enough encouraging signs this season to suggest there’s still plenty of life in him.

Regular watchers of the Bundesliga will tell you how solid Brown is. For everyone else, they discovered him at the World Cup – one of very few individuals to escape from Germany’s desperately disappointing campaign with any credit in the bank.

You can see why Bayern moved quickly to secure his signature. Given Davies’ aforementioned struggles, it was a no-brainer of a signing – the Bavarians foodchaining their domestic competition yet again.

He’s not exactly been a revelation since arriving at the Allianz Arena, but has slotted into Vincent Kompany’s side comfortably enough, contributing a goal and two assists in his first eight Bundesliga appearances. There’s plenty more to come, and if he continues developing under the Belgian, there’s no reason why he can’t establish himself among the very best in his position.

The Manchester City academy graduate has the talent and potential to be challenging for the top end of this list, but things haven’t quite clicked under Enzo Maresca just yet.

He’s been in and out of the team during an underwhelming start to life under the new manager, making it difficult to build any real momentum. We’ve still favoured O’Reilly over Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly, having seen considerably more of him at left-back over the past year.

As with Lewis-Skelly, we suspect O’Reilly’s long-term future might lie in midfield. He certainly possesses the technical skill set to make it happen. But there’s still plenty more work to do before he fulfils his considerable potential.

Manchester United were desperate to sign Hall last summer, but Newcastle stood firm. Given the bin fire they’ve subsequently continued to serve up at Old Trafford, he might consider himself fortunate.

That’s not to say Hall isn’t an excellent young footballer. He’s just no magician, and even his considerable talent hasn’t been enough to elevate Matthias Jaissle’s struggling Newcastle side.

One of those players who could look absolutely sensational in a properly functioning team. We’re still backing him to get there.

Grimaldo played a grand total of zero minutes in Spain’s World Cup triumph.

The former Bayer Leverkusen wingback spoke of his eagerness to play his part, but he’s a bit unfortunate that one of the few better players in his position across world football shares his nationality.

Grimaldo has made an outstanding start to life at Atletico Madrid, quickly establishing himself as one of Diego Simeone’s key players. He’s been a standout performer as Atleti look to challenge Barcelona and Real Madrid for the La Liga title.

Not quite to the same extent as some of the prior names in this list, but we’re still left with a sense that Calafiori’s lack of durability costs him a little.

The Italian heartthrob played a decent amount of football last season – 36 appearances and over 2000 minutes in all competitions – but he still missed vast swathes of Arsenal’s quadruple chase, including much of the Premier League run-in and latter stages of the Champions League knockouts.

Calafiori undoubtedly possesses the ability – particularly on the defensive side of his game – to challenge at the top end of this ranking, and he’s showing it more consistently this season. He’s also offering plenty going forward, an aspect of his game that’s becoming increasingly prominent.

Dimarco suffered such a colossal mare in Inter’s 2025 Champions League final shellacking at the hands of PSG that it’s difficult to imagine his reputation ever fully recovering.

But every footballer has their off days, and if you take that out of the equation and Di Marco’s track record is outstanding. Two Scudetti, three Coppa Italia, runs to two Champions League finals, twice being included in the Serie A Team of the Season.

And it’s not just pedigree. Last season was probably his best yet, having notched seven goals and 17 – yes, seventeen – assists as Inter waltzed to the title. He was deservedly named Serie A’s MVP – how often has that ever happened to a full-back in a top European league?

Inter have had an up-and-down start to this campaign, but he remains one of their best and most important players. Badly missed in the recent Milan derby defeat.

Positionally astute, bit of a sh*thouse, decent enough going forward but never at the expense of his defensive duties. Real Madrid have basically signed Jose Mourinho’s idea of the perfect left-back.

Best of all, he’s a big game player. Three summers in a row he’s shone on the big stage. The European Championship. The Club World Cup. The World Cup. Across all three finals, he didn’t put a foot wrong. He was far too good to be playing in a Chelsea side so dysfunctional.

Cucurella looked exposed and out of sorts during the unconvincing early weeks of Jose Mourinho’s reign, struggling badly in defeat to Atletico Madrid. But he’s grown into the campaign as the new manager has tweaked his way towards a more functional set-up.

He was outstanding in the recent El Clasico win, effectively shutting down Spain team-mate Lamine Yamal. Yan Diomande helping out makes a big difference, and Cucurella will probably be hoping Vini Jr doesn’t reclaim his place any time soon.

The case isn’t quite as cut and dried as with Achraf Hakimi on the opposite flank, but it was nevertheless a pretty easy decision.

Mendes and Hakimi have been integral to Luis Enrique’s PSG winning back-to-back Champions Leagues.

Their defensive ability is the starting point, with both excelling in one-on-one duels, but they are far from limited when it comes to supporting the attack. That all-round skill set forms one of the pillars of a remarkably effective set-up.

#1489. Can you name Real Madrid’s top 20 Champions League goalscorers?

No club has won the Champions League more than Real Madrid so it’s no surprise that the famous club boasts some of the competition’s greatest goalscorers.

Madrid have won the European Cup a record 14 times – eight of which have come since the competition was rebranded as the Champions League in 1992.

During that time, the La Liga club have proudly possessed some of the modern era’s greatest players and most prolific strikers. But can you name their top 20 top goalscorers in Europe’s most prestigious cup competition?

There are three very famous names way out in front, and we’re sure you’d be able to get each of them in your sleep. Things drop off surprisingly dramatically from there, and there are some surprising players that make the list.

This one is actually trickier than you might think, and we’ll be seriously impressed if you can get full marks. An asterisk denotes a player currently still at the club.

If you’re up for another challenge afterwards try name the top scorer for every La Liga season since 1990.

#1487. Palmer and Rogers complete 12-minute rescue mission to save Chelsea

Xabi Alonso needed the cavalry – and referee Jarred Gillett – to stop Chelsea making a quick exit from the Carabao Cup and, boy, did they come up trumps for him.

Chelsea had looked to be heading out of the competition shortly after half-time, but, in Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, Alonso has a cheat code that is capable of masking even the worst defending.

Alonso’s side have shared 26 goals in the five games they have played this season. It has certainly been an entertaining start by Chelsea’s latest manager.

Palmer, Rogers and Pedro Neto stepped off the substitutes’ bench to complete a stunning rescue mission against Leeds United. Palmer scored twice, Neto once and Rogers helped himself to at least a hat-trick of assists. He claimed it was four, but the record books may say three.

When it was announced Palmer had been awarded the player of the match, Rogers responded by saying: “Mate, I got four assists. I can’t believe that! That’s mental. He scored a pen!”

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

Chelsea had looked down and out, when, just three minutes after Alonso’s quadruple half-time change, Leeds doubled their lead. But four goals in an incredible 12-minute spell turned the tie on its head and it was Alonso’s substitutes who Chelsea had to thank.

Palmer, with some help from Gillett, was the first to come to the home side’s rescue. Four minutes after Brenden Aaronson had put Leeds 2-0 up, Gillett pointed to the penalty spot after Daniel James had stood on the foot of Pep Chavarría.

It looked like a harsh decision on Leeds and proved to be almost as big of a game-changer as Alonso’s substitutions. Palmer stepped up to score the resulting penalty.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

“Nobody in the stadium, not one player was asking for a penalty and he gave the penalty,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “All of a sudden their players came into the game. The momentum was on their side. Situations can change the whole momentum of the game.”

Stamford Bridge sensed a comeback and in the 55th minute, Rogers nudged the ball into the path of Palmer who produced a brilliant curling finish to beat Michael Zetterer, the Leeds goalkeeper.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Reece James then went close, before Neto completed the turnaround on the hour mark. Palmer found Rogers, who in turn picked out Neto and he sent Stamford Bridge wild by sending his shot into the corner of the net.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

As Farke waited to make a quadruple substitution of his own, Danny Welbeck got in on the act by collecting the ball from Rogers, spinning and scoring.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

That should have been that and the atmosphere could not have been more different from half-time, when Chelsea fans had booed off their side after watching them fall a goal behind.

Reggie Watson, Chelsea’s 16-year-old debutant, Malo Gusto, Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens were hooked at half-time by Alonso, who said: “For sure, I take responsibility for all of them. No player to blame. It’s the decisions that we took.

“I know that probably I haven’t taken the right decisions for them to show their best level. It’s something that I will analyse and learn from. So it’s my responsibility and we had to make decisions at half-time. And we have seen another second half with another quality.”

Goalkeeper Mike Penders was one of the nine changes made by Alonso. He produced a superb double-save to first keep out Aaronson and then recover to tip Tarik Muharemovic’s header out from the corner.

Conor Coady was impressed with that Mike Penders double save in the first half 👏 pic.twitter.com/6NJqFDvnzk

But the Belgian flapped at the corner, which gave Harry Wilson a second chance to get his delivery right. And he did just that by finding Muharemovic at the back post to head the ball into the net.

Valentín Barco survived Alonso’s changes, but was partly at fault for Leeds’s second goal just after the break. He lost the ball and Ethan Ampadu galloped away from Rogers before crossing. Lukas Nmecha got the slightest of touches and Aaronsen smashed the ball into the net.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

The substitutes then took over, as Chelsea shocked the visitors before Leeds substitute Dominic Calvert-Lewin gave his team hope by reducing the deficit with 15 minutes remaining.

Any thoughts of a Leeds comeback were quickly erased, however, as Barco netted his first Chelsea goal from a Rogers pass, which may have taken a slight touch to deny him a fourth assist in the record books. Welbeck added a sixth in time added on.

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

On the defeat by Chelsea, Farke said: “The referee had the idea to give a penalty. No one in the stadium was asking for it, no one of their players was asking for it, but he spotted a situation where he thought he would give a penalty.

“All of a sudden they scored the goal, then their players came into the game at half-time, the whole stadium after being relatively quiet for 60 minutes they of course were there then. The momentum was all of a sudden on their side. In football small situations can change the whole momentum of a game and this happened.”

"100% I meant it!" 😅Morgan Rogers says he is really enjoying his football after he helped Chelsea beat Leeds 6-3 in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/7uUQb6eIla

Here’s a reminder of the assist in question. Did Rogers mean it? Let us know in the comments beneath this live blog...

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

On the message from the manager at half-time, Palmer told Sky Sports: “Just up the intensity, play a bit more, become more alive because I think the first half was flat, everyone agreed in the changing room, so we stepped up.

Asked whether Alonso’s message was delivered calmly, he said: “At the start, but then he got a bit angry. But it was alright.”

On Chelsea’s half-time changes, Conor Coady said on Sky Sports: “I think the credit goes down to [Alonso]. He made a bit of a statement by doing that at half-time. Four subs is a lot to do at half-time but it was needed. Listen, we said about the first half that it was kind of like the players hadn’t played with each other, and then the big guns came on... They were electric at times.”

A crazy match which was decided by Chelsea’s superb substitutes. Alonso took action at half-time and was rewarded with six goals in a madcap second half. Palmer hauled Chelsea back into the game, Rogers collected a handful of assists and Neto scored the go-ahead goal. You wonder what this match will do for the likes of Estevao and Gittens, though.

Chelsea 6 Leeds United 3 (Welbeck) Pure reflexes from Welbeck, who diverts Barco’s wild effort beyond Zetterer.

Palmer has the hat-trick ball on his mind and attempts an audacious chip but just gets his angles wrong. Any guesses who laid on the chance? Rogers. Of course.

Fans in the away end have resolved they have seen enough and are now heading towards the exits. Stach attempts to launch a counter but his raking cross-field ball is far too heavy.

Rogers drifts out to the left and wins Chelsea a valuable corner. James walks over to take it to rapturous applause from supporters there.

Leeds look to break but Wilson mistimes his run and is caught offside.

There will be six minutes of time added on.

Chance! Okafor darts inside of Neto and spins in a teasing ball to the back post but neither Calvert-Lewin nor Tanaka are able to reach it.

Shouts for a Leeds penalty fail to pique the interest of referee Gillett. Gudmundsson was felled on the left of the box but the contact looked minimal.

A tap on Barco’s head from Wilson provokes some histrionics from the Argentine but Jarred Gillett calms all parties down.

Leeds are still pushing. Stach’s effort from eight yards out is closed down before Tanaka’s strike from the edge of the box is smothered by James.

Alonso goes into the book, apparently for straying too far outside of his technical area.

Chelsea 5 Leeds United 3 (Barco) Rogers lays on his fourth assist of the match, driving towards the byline before flashing a searching ball across the face of goal which Barco spears past Zetterer at the far post. That should be that, right?

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

Gudmundsson replaces debutant Bard down Leeds’ left.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 3 (Calvert-Lewin) Game back on? Okafor is afforded far too much space down the left by a tiring Chelsea back line and his cross finds Calvert-Lewin who plants the ball past Penders to reduce the deficit to just one goal. What a tie this has turned into!

Leeds win a corner, which falls to Stach on the edge of the box but his effort is charged down.

It will be a source of acute anguish for Farke that Chelsea’s fourth goal came before he could make his four changes: Stach, Calvert-Lewin, Tanaka and Okafor eventually replace James, Nmecha, Longstaff and Aaronson. Conversely, it should be to Alonso’s credit that he took action early - his substitutes have decided this tie.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 2 (Welbeck) Rogers gallops on to a simple ball down the right channel and his cutback (towards Palmer) is picked up by Welbeck who spins before firing beyond Zetterer, leaving three Leeds defenders sprawled in front of him. He cares not, and absorbs the love of the crowd in the near corner.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

Palmer goes close after having found a yard of space on the edge of the box. His strike spears through a thicket of limbs in Leeds’ box but Zetterer pulls off a strong save to deny the Englishman a quickfire hat-trick.

Chelsea 3 Leeds United 2 (Neto) Just 11 minutes after going 2-0 down, Chelsea find themselves ahead. Palmer threads a through-ball through the middle for Rogers, who slides in front of his marker to an open Neto who sweeps the ball beyond Zetterer. Leeds punished for leaving themselves two vs two at the back there.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

Chelsea have got their tails up and Palmer almost lays on a go-ahead goal but James cannot turn in his cross from the left.

Chelsea 2 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Wow! Palmer has turned this game on its head. And it’s so, so simple. Acheampong’s throw-in is knocked down by Rogers into the path of Palmer who works in from the right, passing the ball around a Leeds defender and past a rooted Zetterer.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Chelsea 1 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Palmer makes no mistake. He goes right, and while Zetterer guesses the right way he cannot get there and Chelsea are back in business.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

Chavarria is caught by James in the box and the referee points to the spot. That came from nowhere.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 2 (Aaronson) Amapadu deserves so much credit here. He steals the ball from Barco high, bursts beyond Rogers on the right and while Nmecha cannot turn in his cutback, Aaronson arrives late to stroke the ball past Penders and double Leeds’ lead.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

Alonso resolves he has seen enough and rings the changes at the interval. Palmer, Rogers, James and Neto enter the fray in place of Estevao, Watson, Gittens and Gusto.

Big cheers from the Chelsea fans at half-time, as Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto, Morgan Rogers and Reece James have all come on to warm up and are stripped off ready to play. Alonso is sending on the cavalry.

The delayed kick-off has knocked us out of kilter with tonight’s Champions League matches, but here are the live scores:

Liverpool 2 Atletico Madrid 1Paris St-Germain 4 Slovan 0Napoli 0 Arsenal 0Sporting CP 1 Galatasaray 1

Boos at half-time from the Chelsea fans. Their team were pretty awful, but booing so early in the season. Really?

There is only one minute of time added on and Watson earns himself a booking for a late challenge on Wilson before the half-time whistle is blown. It will be interesting to see how long Alonso waits before turning to his bench.

Justin, James and Wilson have got a lot of joy down Leeds’ right, rotating in Chavarria’s orbit. It has been difficult for Chelsea to pin them down and Gittens’ attacking threat has been blunted as he attempts to track their movements.

Better from Chelsea. Watson does well to regain possession high and Estevao takes over, darting towards the by-line. His cutback is directed towards Welbeck but he is beaten to the ball by a Leeds toe and it is played behind for a corner which comes to nothing.

Chelsea are really struggling to build up a head of steam, with individual mistakes proving costly.

Gittens and Estevao both end up on the left and the former works infield before firing a shot at Zetterer which the German parries behind for a corner. Perhaps Chelsea’s most dangerous moment of the half.

The corner is played short with the ball eventually falling to Barco on the edge of the box but his mis-hit effort trickles wide.

Gittens rescues an overhit Acheampong cross and finds Barco on the edge of the box, but the Argentine’s effort is charged down. Leeds spring a counter and their sweeping move up field earns them a corner.

Wilson floats another delivery to the back post to Muharemovic, but he cannot replicate his earlier goal.

Farke will be delighted with what he has seen so far. It is all well and good Chelsea allowing Leeds the ball, but they have to break incisively when openings arise, and they have not done that.

Big chance for Leeds! James bursts down the right and the Welsh winger dinks in a cross to the far post which Justin cannot get past Acheampong, but while Longstaff is first to the second ball, he can only sky the shot over the bar.

Leeds’ goal has stirred something inside them and they look motivated to score a second. Ampadu launches a long throw from the left which ricochets off a couple of players before rolling out for a Chelsea goal-kick.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 1 (Muharemovic) Set-pieces have been a massive feature of Leeds’ game this season and here they take the lead with the simplest of corner routines. Wilson floats the ball to the back post where Muharemovic is waiting, unmarked, and he loops a header over Penders into the net. Such a shame for the Chelsea keeper as he had just pulled off a stunning double-save.

"The set-piece routine does it again!" Tarik Muharemović puts Leeds in front against Chelsea! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/UxeJ3xgL56

Barco slips on the far side and in doing so concedes a corner rather comically, to the delight of the travelling supporters. The delivery is met by Lacroix and Leeds are unable to create anything from the second phase of the set-piece.

There is an intriguing duel developing down Chelsea’s right as Bard looks to contain Estevao. The French wing-back has done a decent job so far.

Estevao attempts to free himself of Bard’s clutches and drifts inside, Chavarria then almost picks him out with a cross from the left but Leeds just about clear their lines.

Justin plays in a cultured through-ball from a wide-right position to James but Chavarria does well to snuff it out. Leeds are making the pitch as big as possible and spaces are beginning to open up as they did at Fulham on the opening weekend.

Although Penders’ shot-stopping has not yet been tested, he has shown some nifty footwork, sweeping up any loose balls that make it past Chelsea’s back three/five.

Big chance! Chelsea spring a surprise attack as Chavarria sets Gittens away down the left. He works the ball infield to Welbeck who lays on a great chance for Estevao but Justin darts back to take the ball off the Brazilian’s toes. A brilliant piece of last-ditch defending.

Gittens gets a shot away, a tame effort straight at Zetterer from 22 yards out as he cuts in from the left. The correct intent, though.

Leeds look to circulate the ball across their back line. As mentioned pre-match, Chelsea will not mind letting their opponents get on the ball as they set out-of-possession traps. Aaronson eventually dribbles off the pitch on the far side.

Chelsea’s Argentine midfielder, Valentin Barco, is being booed by the Leeds fans every time he touches the ball. Barco will already be used to getting that treatment, as it has even happened to him while he’s been a substitute this season.

In other news, there’s a real Borussia Dortmund vibe to this Leeds away kit.

Leeds supporters boo Argentina World Cup squad member Barco’s every touch, and another Leeds foul, this time Justin on Gittens, prompts a second Chelsea free-kick.

A couple of early touches for Watson who plays a neat pass around the corner. Ampadu then lands a late tackle on Lacroix and Chelsea earn a free-kick in their own half.

Although there are still some empty seats, we are finally under way. Chelsea in their customary all blue, kicking from right to left. Leeds in their yellow away strip.

Chelsea and Leeds emerge from the tunnel, led out by Colwill and former Chelsea defender Ampadu. Here’s a reminder of the teams in full:

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Daniel Farke believes Leeds can go far in the Carabao Cup this year 💪 pic.twitter.com/26ueAAUHoZ

On the Brazilian winger’s opportunity tonight, Hasselbaink said on Sky Sports: “He has to find his place. This is his opportunity... It’s not really an out-and-out left-wing [position] or a No 10 as he can play, but [with] good players it doesn’t matter where you put them on the pitch. He will find his spaces and he will be direct as he was when he came in against Arsenal. He is going to play for his place because he wants to play week-in, week-out.”

"He deserves to be there because of what he has shown" Xabi Alonso speaks about Reggie Watson with the 16-year-old set to make his Chelsea debut in their Carabao Cup game against Leeds 🌟 pic.twitter.com/AAn4Av3iEh

Tfl has closed South Kensington station after a “customer incident” meaning parts of the District Line have closed. The decision was then made to delay the match to give supporters more time to get to the stadium.

Reggie Watson will become the fourth youngest player, aged 16, in Chelsea’s history. But he will have to wait a little bit longer for his debut as kick-off has been delayed by 15 minutes to 8.15pm.

There will be a 15 minute delay to kick-off for our Carabao Cup third round tie with Leeds United tonight. The match will now begin at 20:15 BST. pic.twitter.com/MdDXpxgW09

A couple of cracking strikes from the Dutchman. Some player he was...

"Good old days!" Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink reflects on his goals for Leeds against Chelsea 🎞️ pic.twitter.com/bYjyFYIVIK

ChelseaAug 24: Fulham 2 Chelsea 3Aug 27: Chelsea 2 Luton Town 0 (Carabao Cup)Aug 30: Chelsea 4 Brighton 3Sep 6: Arsenal 2 Chelsea 1

LeedsAug 22: Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds 1Aug 25: Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds 2Aug 30: Leeds 1 Brentford 1Sep 5: Brighton 1 Leeds 1

As recently as March, a giant mural of Estêvão Willian appeared on the side of a building outside Stamford Bridge as the teenager threatened to become Chelsea’s number one poster boy.

He may no longer hold top billing outside the club, following a summer in which Chelsea spent a club-record £117m on Morgan Rogers to complete a fearsome front three alongside Cole Palmer and João Pedro.

A giant mural of the Brazilian teenager appeared on the side of a building close to Stamford Bridge in March.

But inside Stamford Bridge, nothing has changed. Estêvão remains one of Chelsea’s star boys and is part of an “untouchable” group of players that also includes Palmer, Rogers and Pedro. Sources believe Estêvão is a player the club will look at rewarding with an improved contract in the coming months.

Having already earned his Chelsea “untouchable” status, the next challenge for the 19-year-old winger – once nicknamed “Messinho” – is to make himself undroppable.

Estêvão may not be a perfect fit for Xabi Alonso’s three-at-the-back formation that features two 10s – Palmer and Rogers – behind a striker. But the boy from Brazil is certainly not being squeezed out and Chelsea’s manager has spoken of the need to be flexible.

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Much has been made of Chelsea’s willingness to let the opposition have the ball under Xabi Alonso, but tonight they will likely be forced to dictate proceedings. In Leeds, they face one of only two sides who have completed fewer passes than them in the Premier League.

1. Ian Hamilton in 1967: 16 years, four months and 15 days2. Kingsley Whiffen in 1967: 16 years, five months and six days3. Reggie Walsh in 2025: 16 years, six months and 11 days4. Reggie Watson in 2026: 16 years, seven months and 14 days5. Tommy Langley in 1974: 16 years, nine months and one day

Asked how he will approach the Carabao Cup this season, Daniel Farke said: “We’ll try to win it. That’s the quickest way to Europe and to some glory. Of course knowing that the Premier League will always have the priority and knowing that we are as successful as possible there, especially to reach our first goal to establish ourselves [at] this level.

“We are not the favourites to win the Carabao Cup, we know this. Challenging, difficult games, but of course we travel to London in order to go through in the next round without doing anything stupid at this stage of the campaign because you also have to rotate a bit more and integrate a few new players. Nevertheless, we want to be at our best and anyhow possible we also want to go through to the next round.”

Tonight represents an opportunity for 16-year-old Reggie Watson to announce himself at senior level. The central-midfielder caught Alonso’s eye during pre-season when the Spaniard said of him: “Reggie Watson, a great midfielder. He thinks, he’s very collective, he’s very generous on the effort, intelligent with the ball”.

“For his age, I’m really impressed with him.”

Dan James passes a late fitness test to make Daniel Farke’s starting XI.

📋 Tonight's Starting XI pic.twitter.com/MQKQtGZm8c

Reggie Watson, 16, son of former Wigan midfielder Ben (of 2013 FA Cup final fame), makes his full Chelsea debut and becomes the club’s fourth youngest player. Estevao, Jamie Gittens and Danny Welbeck replace Alonso’s thrilling forward three, who are on the bench.

Chelsea XI Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Your Blues to face Leeds United in the #CarabaoCup! #CFC pic.twitter.com/636SOiUXVB

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of tonight’s Carabao Cup third-round tie between Chelsea and Leeds United. This is a rematch of last season’s FA Cup semi-final which Chelsea edged by a single Enzo Fernández goal, but plenty has changed since then. Xabi Alonso has taken over the reins at Stamford Bridge and made a promising start, reeling off three wins before losing to Arsenal in an absorbing contest last Sunday. Chelsea are not involved in European competition this season, so the domestic cups represent an avenue to silverware, as well as an opportunity to tinker.

In Alonso’s way, though, stands a Leeds team whose manager, Daniel Farke, told the media on Tuesday that his side are aiming to win the Carabao Cup. Farke has overseen an impressive run of form, having lost only two of their previous 16 competitive matches in a stretch that extends back to March. Two wins at Nottingham Forest preceded draws against Brentford and Brighton to keep Leeds undefeated this term. Farke has suggested he will rotate in west London to “integrate new players” having brought in seven new recruits during the summer.

If Leeds are to reach the next round, they must reverse a heavily one-sided head-to-head record against their hosts, who have won each of their past 10 cup meetings (three in the League Cup, seven in the FA Cup). In fact, Chelsea have lost at this stage of the competition just once in the past 15 years, and that was against Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City four seasons ago.

Alonso broke up the exhilarating “JP Morgan” band (João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers) for Chelsea’s victory over Luton Town in the previous round, handing starts to Danny Welbeck and Estêvão. Players such as Jamie Gittens and Geovany Quenda are also waiting in the wings and may get chances to impress tonight. Mike Penders could also be in line for a start between the sticks.

#1486. Erik ten Hag launches latest attack on Cristiano Ronaldo: Former Man United boss claims Portugal star's career was OVER by time he joined Juventus

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 12:32 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EDT, 1 November 2026

Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has taken another swipe at Cristiano Ronaldo, claiming the Portugal icon's career was already over by the time he joined Juventus and eventually returned to Old Trafford.

The legendary forward's second spell at United ended acrimoniously after he launched a public attack on the club and Ten Hag, accusing the manager of 'betraying' him in a bombshell interview.

Ronaldo, whose United contract was terminated following his explosive criticism of the club, joined Al-Nassr in January 2023, while Ten Hag was eventually sacked in October 2024 after a disappointing run of results.

Last month, Ten Hag gave a wide-ranging interview to The Athletic in which he criticised Ronaldo for 'letting the team down' and accused the club's hierarchy of contributing to a 'toxic culture'.

The Dutchman has now doubled down on his criticism of the 41-year-old veteran once again, claiming Ronaldo could not 'make way' for the team.

'Every top team must embrace the top player, but the top player must also make way for the team. That was simply the problem with Ronaldo,' Ten Hag said in an interview on ESPN.

Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo's career was over by the time he returned to United

Ten Hag conducted a wide-ranging interview with The Athletic last week in which he hit out at the club's hierarchy for contributing to a 'toxic culture' - and lashed out at Ronaldo

'Let there be no misunderstanding on my part, he is of course a great player. He belongs among the greats of the world.

'But the reality is also that he hasn't been able to deliver for the last seven or eight years. From Juventus onwards, it was simply over.'

Ten Hag also praised Real Madrid, where Ronaldo statistically enjoyed the most prolific years of his career, for selling the superstar at what he believed was the perfect time.

'That is also Real Madrid's great gift,' he added. 'They see when a player is declining in level. Then they part ways at a moment when, to the outside world, they are still at their peak, but actually can no longer deliver.'

In Ten Hag's tell-all interview last month, he accused Manchester United's owners of 'breaking promises' over recruitment and blasted them for showing a lack of ambition in the transfer market.

His criticism of Manchester United came amid a turbulent spell for the club, with Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes both publicly criticising the board and manager Michael Carrick respectively in recent weeks.

Carrick was given a chance to put things right after United's chiefs met for crunch talks earlier this week in the wake of his side losing 4-1 to Como in the Champions League and 3-0 to Bournemouth in the Premier League.

According to Ten Hag, Ronaldo was not prepared to stand aside for the good of the team

Ronaldo, who now plays for Al-Nassr, is within touching distance of scoring 1,000 career goals

On Saturday, United met a similar fate as they were thumped 3-0 by Chelsea at Stamford Bridge, piling even more pressure on Carrick.

Red Devils legend Peter Schmeichel expressed his anger at Ten Hag speaking out against the club during this difficult period last week.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily, former United goalkeeper Schmeichel said: 'What really annoys me in everything that has happened in the past two weeks is Ten Hag coming out and saying that he wanted Declan Rice and Harry Kane, like he was a god.

'It's so ridiculous. He brought (Lisandro) Martinez in, (Matthijs) de Ligt. I mean he brought players in that are still there, how dare he go out and say that.

'Everybody knew we should sign Harry Kane. Everyone knows we should have signed Declan Rice, that's no secret. I don't know why we didn't do that.

'But you have now people stirring the pot where they should just keep calm and not talk and maybe talk about what they did for this football club themselves, or what they didn't do.

'He wasn't a success at Manchester United. Why does he feel the need to come out and say that?

'What he's saying is "I was let down by the club" and there might be an element of truth in that but he wasn't good enough. And then he went to Bayer Leverkusen, a team who had just won the Bundesliga, and then he got sacked within, what, three games?

Ten Hag also hit out at Manchester United's hierarchy amid a turbulent time for the club

Michael Carrick has been given a chance to turn things around after chiefs held crunch talks

'Maybe just take a step back and don't put yourself in that because then you will end up with someone like me criticising him, and there's no need for that. We don't need it in the narrative.'

Ten Hag was sacked by United in October 2024 after a string of poor results left the team 14th in the Premier League.

His future had been in doubt after he led United to a disappointing eighth-placed finish in the top flight a couple of months earlier, but victory in the FA Cup final over rivals Manchester City contributed to the club's decision to give him a contract extension in the summer after crunch talks in Ibiza.

He went on to replace Xabi Alonso at Bundesliga side Bayer Leverkusen the following season, but was sacked after just three games in charge, and he criticised the club's board for this 'unprecedented' decision.

#1485. Michael Carrick is the latest Man Utd boss to save his job with one result

Michael Carrick may have saved his Manchester United job after they overcame a 2-0 deficit to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League.

For the first time since early September, United fans can celebrate a win and it is a result that may have saved Carrick’s job, for now.

Here are four other times United managers were given a stay of execution by a single result.

It’s the example that gets brought up every time a current Manchester United manager is struggling.

Ferguson was three years into his Manchester United tenure and things were not going so well.

A second-place finish was sandwiched between two 11th-place finishes; they would end the 1989-90 season in 13th and general consensus was Ferguson was not long for the sack.

It was a season which had seen United lose 5-1 away at their noisy neighbours. In December, a banner was unfurled, reading “3 Years Of Excuses And It’s Still Crap. Ta Ra Fergie”. Calls for the sack were growing by the day.

But it was the FA Cup that rescued the future great. United were away at Nottingham Forest in the third round and there was the hope that going on an elongated cup run may distract the Old Trafford faithful from the league form.

Their opponents were Brian Clough’s Forest, a fading giant but still a club that won two European Cups within recent memory. Ferguson made a selection gamble, playing 20-year-old striker Mark Robins and it worked.

The future Coventry manager grabbed the only goal of the game to put United through. They would go on to win the tournament and give Ferguson some much-needed breathing room.

That goal kickstarted the era that would see every trophy come to Old Trafford. United finished sixth the following season. The year after that they were second before winning the first Premier League season in 1993.

Carrick’s success is not the first time United have overcome a 2-0 deficit in Europe to save a manager’s job.

United had started the 2021-22 season poorly under Solskjaer. They had been knocked out of the League Cup. They had been beaten by Young Boys in the Champions League. They had won just one of their past five games and had most recently been thumped 4-2 by Leicester.

The boos that rang out at Old Trafford following a 1-1 draw at Everton showed that the usually patient home fans had turned on their 1999 hero.

And then Solskjaer’s P45 was practically being written up when United trailed Atalanta 2-0 after half an hour.

But a second-half comeback finished off by Cristiano Ronaldo gave Solskjaer a stay of execution, if only for a little while.

They lost the next game 5-0 to Liverpool but persevered with Solskjaer, who took them to second.

He was sacked after a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November.

By all reports, United were ready to sack Ten Hag that evening before he unexpectedly beat Manchester City in the FA Cup final.

United were rank outsiders when facing Pep Guardiola’s City, who had just won their fourth consecutive Premier League title, and yet saved their performance of the season for their final match of the season.

Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring on the half-hour mark before Kobbie Mainoo made it two nine minutes later. Ten Hag had outthought Pep, allowing City to have the ball before countering at pace. Jeremy Doku got one back but it was not enough to stop United winning their 13th FA Cup.

It was a moment that many hoped would parallel Ferguson, perhaps this could be what changed United’s fortunes. It wasn’t.

Ten Hag had finished eighth with them but widespread reports of his sacking had undermined any credibility the Dutchman had at the club.

Ten Hag had also given the green light to some of the worst signings in United history, particularly the £86 million paid to Ajax for Antony.

He was eventually sacked in October, just five months after the FA Cup win and delaying the decision cost United even more. Ruben Amorim, a man with a completely different system, was brought in mid-season and never recovered.

A League Cup exit at the hands of Derby and a 3-1 defeat to West Ham had Mourinho on the brink at United.

It was typical late-stage Mourinho. He had fallen out with a number of his own players, most notably Paul Pogba, and there was a cloud of toxicity suffocating the club.

When United went 2-0 down inside the opening 10 minutes against Newcastle at home, that looked to be the end of it.

But United woke up 20 minutes before time. Juan Mata, the much-maligned player under Mourinho at two successive clubs, had curled in a free kick. Anthony Martial equalised in the 76th minute.

And then Alexis Sanchez scored a dramatic late winner to give United the win and complete the comeback.

The fans cheered Mourinho’s name, but it only delayed the end rather than stopping it outright.

United drew the next game 2-2 to Chelsea but went on a run that saw them lose to Juventus, City and Liverpool. That 3-1 defeat at Anfield was enough for Mourinho to be given his marching orders.
